h: Welcome to the EO Brand Guidelines
t: Welcome to the EO Brand Guidelines
b: EO is a media brand for builders. It rallies builders (Rallying), stands with builders of conviction (Conviction), and has their backs (Backing). Recording the founder's journey as it is, and carrying that story to the next builder: that is what EO does. These guidelines describe the fundamental elements of the EO identity system: logo · typography · color · graphic system. Their purpose is to make the brand's content and services look and read as one EO, in San Francisco · Seoul · Vietnam alike. Some slides may use exceptional expressions or combinations for the sake of explanation; where a slide and the text differ, the text takes precedence. Build Anyway. The EO Brand Team

EO · the EO symbol · the signature · the sub symbol · "Build Anyway" · "Entrepreneur Onwards" and other trademarks owned by EO Studio (hereafter the EO Logos ), together with the brand's distinctive aesthetic features such as graphic units · patterns · EO's look and feel (hereafter the Brand Assets), are the exclusive property of EO Studio. Except as permitted here, any use of the EO Logos or Brand Assets requires the prior permission of EO Studio.

Always follow these brand guidelines when using the EO Logos and Brand Assets. You may use the EO Logos to indicate that you have appeared in EO content or taken part in an EO program. Do not, however, give the impression that EO endorses or sponsors your product or service. When citing EO videos and articles, credit the source clearly as "EO" and provide a link to the original. Use the EO Logos and Brand Assets only as provided in the original files, unaltered, and only within the approved color combinations.

Do not include the EO Logos, or any logo confusingly similar to them, in a company · product · service · event · community name, URL, social media account, or trademark. Do not alter or recombine the EO symbol · graphic units · patterns for use as your own graphics. Do not re-edit or re-upload EO's videos · articles · thumbnails without EO's permission. Do not copy or imitate the look and feel (layout · color combinations · typefaces · graphic system) of EO's website · magazine · social channels. Do not use the EO Logos alongside political · religious messages · adult content · discriminatory content. Do not use the EO Logos or Brand Assets on merchandise without permission.

The EO logo is the umbrella term for the EO symbol · signature · EO sub symbol covered in this chapter. This page describes how to apply the EO symbol across situations · formats · communications, from a small sign-off to large-scale display use.

A graphic metaphor that makes the brand recognizable through a screw motif, and a monogram logo that holds the two letters E and O. This form of the logo is hereafter called the EO symbol . The EO symbol is the most iconic and effective way to signal the media brand EO.

The EO symbol is designed around the three parts of a screw: shaft · thread · head. Thread — One turn of the thread stands for a cycle of problem solving. Shaft — The shaft stands for the process of building and the builder's journey, and expresses the courage to keep moving forward (Build Anyway). Head — The head stands for a single small problem solved, or a single builder.

The E block, which depicts the facade of a screw, consists of a shaft and three threads, the basic geometry of the graphic unit . The O block is an octagonal screw head pierced by a cross-shaped hole. Set side by side, the two blocks stand for "Entrepreneur Onwards".

Clearspace is the minimum safeguard that protects the symbol when it sits next to other visual elements such as typography · graphic units · images · the edge of the page. With H as the vertical height of one E block, always keep a clearspace of at least H/2 on all four sides between the symbol and every adjacent element. Because the visual weight of the EO symbol drifts to the left the smaller it is seen, correct it by narrowing the right clearspace. The amount of correction is set by the seen size S. S is the symbol height (mm) converted to a viewing distance of 500mm: calculate it as actual height × 500 ÷ viewing distance, or use the Symbol height value of the logo generator as is. Right clearspace = H × (0.42 + 0.0012 × S), based on the symbol's allowed size range of 4-25mm. Where the clearspace box is centered in a frame, such as an app icon or profile image, the symbol moves right by (H/2 − right clearspace) ÷ 2, and the generator's Right side correction applies this value automatically. For how to apply it, see App & Social Icons .

The EO symbol is designed and tested to work across a range of sizes. Every size rule is based not on the actual pixel · print size but on the height seen by the eye at a distance of 500mm; for media viewed from farther away, apply it to the height converted to the end user's typical viewing distance (actual height × 500 ÷ distance). For the viewing distance of each medium, refer to the Medium presets of the logo generator ; for physical media whose viewing distance varies, we recommend converting at a distance the designer judges from the end user's main usage environment. Optimal range — A height of 40-70px (about 8-15mm) on a 16-inch Mac display viewed from 500mm. Relative to viewing distance, this is 1/60-1/33 of the distance; on other media, scale by this ratio. The optical correction of the thread angle is also tuned to this range. Recommended maximum size — A height of 70px (about 15mm, 1/33 of the viewing distance), the top of the optimal range. We recommend not using the symbol larger than this. Sizes above it are a range prepared for cases that still need a larger symbol. Minimum size — A seen height of 4mm (20px, 1/125 of the viewing distance), on screen and in print alike. Below this, the threads of the E block blur together, so ask the EO design team to review. Maximum size — A height of 125px (about 25mm, 1/20 of the viewing distance). Avoid using it larger than this wherever possible. Any larger and the symbol reads as a flat shape rather than a graphic. When you need a stronger presence, use the graphic pattern instead of the symbol.

The EO symbol is a strong but simple shape. On typical pages, we therefore recommend using it as a sign-off in one of the four corners of the content area. In a video thumbnail that invites the click, the main content should be the protagonist; on a poster that catches the eye, the graphic pattern should be. The symbol's presence should step back to let them lead. As a sign-off, place the symbol in the corner farthest from the person or graphic pattern that is the protagonist of the layout, with appropriate space from the other visual elements around it. This keeps symbol placement simple and consistent, while leaving enough flexibility to accommodate a dynamic graphic system.

When using the symbol for display, do not raise its visual hierarchy simply by scaling it up. Leave ample space around the symbol, so that it keeps its impact at a moderate size. Ideally, the symbol's actual footprint is 5-10% of the whole empty space, and the nearest element is kept at least 2-3 times the symbol's width away. Ideally, a symbol at 5-10% of the empty space it sits in Generous space around the symbol gives it ample presence at a moderate size Do not fill the empty space with the symbol alone Do not place the symbol where there is not enough space around it

The EO symbol has six basic color combinations. Always render the symbol in a single color, and when you are unsure of the background color, use one of the following. 1 Space Black on Builder Neon 2 Air White on Space Black 3 Air White on Solid Gray 4 Space Black on Air White 5 Builder Neon on Space Black 6 Builder Neon on Solid Gray

The EO symbol is built by default as a light symbol in bright colors such as Builder Neon · Air White on dark backgrounds such as Space Black · Solid Gray . If you simply invert the colors to use a dark symbol on a light background, an optical illusion makes the shape look smaller and the gaps look wider. In that case, convert the light symbol in the following order. Scale each of the two blocks up proportionally by H/30 in all four directions. The cross inside the O block keeps its original size. Offset the outline by H/60. The outer edges of the blocks move outward, and the cross moves inward. Reduce the gap between the two enlarged blocks from the original (4/30)H to (3/30)H to complete the dark symbol. This converts a light symbol of any size into a dark symbol of the same level. On a light background, clearspace also looks larger than it is, so keep the clearspace area of the light symbol of the same level unchanged and center the dark symbol within it.

The EO symbol must always read clearly over photography, so overlay an Air White symbol on images with sufficient contrast. If an image is too bright or has overly white areas, the symbol risks being lost in the composition. In that case, overlay a gradient or black box at about 30% opacity before applying the symbol. The composition of the photo should be simple enough for the symbol to stand out. Images that are overly complex, or that have their key subject dead center, become confusing once the symbol is placed on them. With this in mind, choose images, or adjust the image position in relation to the logo. The guidance in this section focuses on overlays on still images rather than on video sequences whose composition changes. The symbol placed where it has sufficient contrast with the background When a photo with uneven brightness must be used, a gradient overlay at about 30% opacity secures contrast Do not let the silhouette of an object in the photo overlap the edge of the symbol Do not place the symbol where it lacks contrast with the photo

The image below shows the basic horizontal lockup of the EO symbol with the logos of partner brands and collaborators. Optically adjust the elements so that they appear the same size. After matching the size of each logo, insert a gap and a vertical divider · collaboration mark between them. Based on the width of one E block (W), the gap between the EO symbol and the partner logo is 1.5W with a divider and 2W with a collaboration mark. Always keep the two logos optically centered vertically.

The image below shows the basic vertical lockup of the EO symbol with the logos of partner brands and collaborators. Optically adjust the elements so that they appear the same size. After matching the size of each logo, insert a horizontal divider between them. The gap between the EO symbol and the partner logo is 1.5H, where H is the height of the EO symbol. Always keep the two logos optically centered horizontally.

A partner brand's logo sometimes does not balance perfectly when aligned with the EO symbol. Because the EO symbol is wide and heavy, a thin or tall partner logo looks smaller even at the same mathematical height. In such cases, optically scale the partner logo up or down to create a more equal hierarchy.

Because the EO symbol is asymmetric, its visual weight shifts to the left the smaller it is seen. In an app icon or profile image, do not simply center the symbol itself; center the clearspace box from Clearspace in the icon area instead. The correction for the icon area's size and viewing distance follows the clearspace rule.
The image below shows the EO symbol applied to an app icon.

To keep the EO symbol consistent and strong, do not reinterpret, alter, or decorate it. This page shows examples of alterations to avoid. When the company name must appear, use the EO signature instead of the symbol. When a sub-brand needs to be identified, create a Service Signature in consultation with the EO design team. Do not stretch or distort the symbol Do not rotate the symbol Do not add an outline to the symbol Do not use a black outline on a light background Do not use a version in which the number of threads in the E, the angle of the O, or the gap between the blocks has changed (such as a still from the logo animation) Do not apply visual effects such as glow · shadow · gradient to the symbol Do not make the symbol so large that it fills most of the space it sits in Do not create graphics by joining or simply repeating the symbol Do not add arbitrary context around the symbol without the permission of the EO design team

The signature is a combination logo that pairs the EO symbol with the text of a company or service name, horizontally or vertically. This page describes how to apply the EO signature across situations · formats · communications. The combination logo that pairs the symbol with the text "EO Studio" is hereafter called the Company Signature , and a combination logo that pairs the symbol with a service name is called a Service Signature . Where the company itself steps forward, such as contracts · proposals · official documents · job postings · website footers, prefer the Company Signature. For each service's brand communication, prefer its Service Signature. Everywhere else the media brand EO must be signaled, such as videos · thumbnails · social posts · posters · content sign-offs, prefer the EO symbol.

The text part of the signature, excluding the symbol, is called the descriptor . Any word, whether a company name · service name · domain, follows the specifications below exactly. The height (H) and width (W) of one E block of the symbol are the basis for every size setting. When the first or last letter of the descriptor is a glyph with a curved side, such as S · o, keep the text left aligned on its baseline and temporarily replace it with H if it is uppercase or h if it is lowercase, to set the edge of the cap box. For example, "Studio" takes its left edge from "Htudio" and its right edge from "Studih". Always get approval from the EO design team when creating a new descriptor or changing an existing one. Do not use temporary names, such as those of campaigns or events, as descriptors. Vertical — set in Founders Grotesk Regular, type size 0.47H, letterspacing 0. Place the top of the cap box H/5 below the bottom edge of the symbol, center it on the symbol, then shift it left by H/100. This is because the E block of the EO symbol has the higher tonal value, which shifts the visual center to the left. Horizontal — set in Founders Grotesk Regular, type size 1.3H, letterspacing 0, with a separate letterspacing of -6% applied only to the space characters between words. Place the left side of the cap box W/2 from the right edge of the symbol, and raise the baseline H/10 above the bottom edge of the symbol.

The signature also needs space around it, on the same principle as the EO symbol. The amount of space, however, differs by form. Vertical — with H as the vertical height of one E block, keep a clearspace of at least H/2 on all four sides around the whole signature. Horizontal — with H as the vertical height of one E block, keep a clearspace of at least H on all four sides around the whole signature.

As on the Symbol page, sizes on this page are given as the symbol height on a 16-inch Mac display (about 5px/mm) viewed from 500mm. On other media, convert using the ratio in parentheses (symbol height relative to viewing distance). The smaller the signature is seen, the more the symbol and descriptor read as a single mass; the larger it is seen, the more each letter of the descriptor comes into focus. The form therefore depends on the visible size, and the threshold is a symbol height of 10mm (50px, 1/50). At the 10mm threshold itself, both the horizontal · vertical forms can be used. At 10mm (50px, 1/50) and below, use the horizontal signature. The horizontal form keeps the symbol and descriptor evenly visible even at small sizes. Above 6mm (30px, 1/80), the space between the words of "EO Studio" becomes noticeable, and the signature can appear split into three masses: symbol · EO · Studio. Within the 6-10mm range, consider using the "Studio" version as an alternative. At 10mm and above, use the vertical signature. From this size, the descriptor of the vertical form reads clearly. The recommended maximum size is a symbol height of 70px (about 15mm, 1/33), and the maximum is a symbol height of 25mm (125px, 1/20). As with the minimum size of the symbol, do not use the signature below 4mm (20px, 1/125) either.
The vertical Company Signature centers "EO Studio" beneath the EO symbol. For its construction, see the vertical specifications in Descriptor .

The horizontal Company Signature places "EO Studio" to the right of the EO symbol. For its construction, see the horizontal specifications in Descriptor . For anyone who has encountered EO before, the EO symbol may already read as "EO", so consider using only "Studio" in the descriptor of the horizontal form.

Examples of the vertical Service Signature. All are built to the same descriptor specifications; check that they read as one family even though the names differ. 1 EO Studio · company 2 EO Magazine · web magazine 3 EO Planet · community 4 EO Newsletter · newsletter

Examples of the horizontal Service Signature. All are built to the same descriptor specifications; check that they read as one family even though the names differ. 1 EO Studio · company 2 EO Magazine · web magazine 3 EO Planet · community 4 EO Newsletter · newsletter

Choose between the signature and the EO symbol by who is speaking. Use the signature where the company EO Studio, or a service the company runs, is the speaker, and the EO symbol for content from EO as a media brand. Use only one of the two in a single deliverable. Because the signature carries text, it needs more room than the EO symbol. Where the space is too small for the text to read clearly, use the EO symbol alone instead of the signature. If you are unsure, first check whether the deliverable truly needs the company name EO Studio. If it does not, the EO symbol is enough. If you are still unsure, ask the EO design team. The signature on emails · official documents and other materials that speak for the company Do not use the signature as a content sign-off The EO symbol used as a content sign-off Do not use the signature and the EO symbol together in one deliverable

The signature uses four of the six color combinations of the EO symbol. Always render the symbol and the type in the same color. 1 Air White on Space Black 2 Air White on Solid Gray 3 Space Black on Air White 4 Space Black on Builder Neon

Like the symbol, the signature is built by default as a light signature in Air White on dark backgrounds such as Space Black · Solid Gray . If you simply invert the colors to use a dark signature on a light background, an optical illusion makes the symbol look thinner and more spread out, and the letters of the descriptor look one step lighter despite the same weight. Vertical — Convert the light symbol by the Symbol › Inversion rules, and center it in both x · y where the light symbol was. Keep the descriptor centered in its original cap box position, with the baseline in its original position. Keep the weight at Regular and invert only the color, then set the type size to 0.48H · letterspacing to -1%, and finish by offsetting the outline outward by H/200. Horizontal — Convert the light symbol by the same rules, and center it in both x · y where the light symbol was. Left align the descriptor to the left edge of the original cap box, with the baseline in its original position. Keep the weight at Regular and invert only the color, then set the type size to 1.35H · letterspacing to -2% (-7% for the space characters between words), and finish by offsetting the outline outward by H/200. This keeps the tonal value balance between the symbol and the descriptor on a light background the same as in the light signature. Center the finished dark signature in x · y on the clearspace of the light signature of the same level, and use it as is.

The EO signature can be locked up with the logos of partner brands and collaborators. The images in this section show examples of the basic lockup. Optically adjust the elements so that they appear the same size. After matching the size of each logo, you can insert a gap and a divider · collaboration mark between them. Based on the width of one E block (W), set the gap between the EO signature and the partner logo to 1.5W with a divider and 2W with a collaboration mark.

The EO signature can also be locked up vertically with the logos of partner brands and collaborators. On the right is an example of the basic vertical lockup. Optically adjust the elements so that they appear the same size. After matching the size of each logo, you can insert a gap and a divider between them. Set the gap between the two logos to 1.5 times the EO symbol height (H), and place the divider horizontally at its center. Always keep the logos optically centered.

The signature is a fixed combination with a defined relationship between symbol and descriptor. Do not change or rebuild its components separately. Do not use the vertical signature at a size so small that the descriptor is hard to read Do not use the horizontal signature at a symbol height above 10mm (50px, 1/50) Do not use a different typeface for the descriptor Do not change the font settings of the descriptor Do not break the descriptor onto multiple lines Do not combine the sub symbol with a descriptor Do not color the symbol and the descriptor differently Do not stretch or distort the signature Do not apply glow · shadow · gradient effects Do not reduce legibility by placing the signature over complex images

The form that uses the E block · O block detached from the symbol is hereafter called the sub symbol . Use it only in very small square spaces where the full EO symbol is hard to recognize, such as favicons · pin badges. Where the size varies by medium, such as app icons · social media avatars, the EO symbol is the default. The designer decides whether to switch to the sub symbol based on the actual visible size, and the EO design team reviews the decision. The sub symbol cannot fully replace the EO symbol, so always use the EO symbol where there is enough room. Because the E block shares its geometry with the graphic unit , it connects naturally to the whole graphic system even at small sizes.

The sub symbol also needs space around it, on the same basis as the EO symbol. With t as the height of one thread element, always keep a clearspace of at least t on all four sides between the symbol and every adjacent element. The clearspace is based on a Builder Neon sub symbol on a Space Black background. Because the O block has a lower tonal value than the E block, a separate 1.04x correction is applied.

The sub symbol uses only two combinations, Builder Neon on Space Black · Space Black on Builder Neon, and each element is always rendered in a single color. In very small spaces such as favicons, optical distortion grows large relative to the size of the shape, so when inverting the colors, scale each block up by 1.1x. 1 Builder Neon on Space Black 2 Space Black on Builder Neon
The image below shows the EO sub symbol applied to a favicon.

The sub symbol is part of the EO symbol and follows the same principles. Do not alter its shape or decorate it, and do not use it outside its defined purposes. Do not stretch or distort the sub symbol Do not rotate the sub symbol Do not flip the sub symbol horizontally Do not add an outline to the sub symbol Do not adjust the clearspace arbitrarily Do not use the sub symbol as a standalone identity in place of the EO symbol

EO's typefaces are Semibold · Medium · Regular · Light · Mono Regular · Mono Light of the Founders Grotesk family. Founders Grotesk reinterprets the early-20th-century grotesques of Miller & Richard and Caslon, and its simple geometry, narrow apertures and tight letterspacing make it read like solid blocks at large sizes. Firm and clear, yet with humanist touches in its details, it matches EO's attitude — serious, but pursuing creativity. The family also has a monospaced typeface that can evoke the builder's motifs, such as engineering · spec sheets. Each weight has a fixed role. Use Medium for display and headlines, Regular for sub-headlines, Light for body copy, and Mono Regular for informational text. For the detailed criteria, see Reference Scale .

The following image shows most of the characters of Founders Grotesk Medium. Medium is the default weight for display and headlines. It supports Latin Extended characters, including Vietnamese tone marks. For scripts it does not support, such as Hangul, use the typefaces in Multilingual .

The following image shows most of the characters of Founders Grotesk Regular. Regular is the default weight for sub-headlines (D2 · H2 · H3), bridging the hierarchy between the Medium of headlines and the Light of body copy. In brand communication with short body copy, such as posters · banners, it also serves as body copy at the level directly below the display headline.

The following image shows most of the characters of Founders Grotesk Light. Light is the default weight for body copy. At large sizes its thin strokes look as if they float, so do not use it for display or headlines.

The following image shows most of the characters of Founders Grotesk Mono Regular. As a monospaced typeface, it readily recalls builder motifs such as engineering · spec sheets, so it can serve as a supporting device that enriches a layout. Use it for tags · dates · reading time · color specs · caption numbers, and not for headlines or body copy.

EO typography is a baseline grid framework measured and scaled from the space type occupies , not from type settings. Set the value of the Line Unit (the base leading, that is, the absolute height between lines), then set each level's leading as a multiple (x) of it; the type size follows automatically by dividing the leading by the linespacing (leading ÷ type size). Separating the setting of hierarchy from the matching of tonal value gives an easier point of entry when a project's typography system has to be built from scratch. When switching to another language , the space type occupies stays the same even if the typeface or type size changes, so layout variation is minimal, and adjusting only the tonal value keeps the look and feel consistent. Switching between dark and light mode has the same advantage. In an AI Assisted Design workflow, two levels of decision can be separated: the AI's efficient layout building and the designer's eye. Leave the broad hierarchy that follows the content logic to the AI, and refine the visual finish through the separately held values, such as linespacing. Read this chapter in the order the framework is carried out. If you need values ready to use, see the presets in Reference Scale . If you are building anew, set the Line Unit following Line Unit and set up the typography through the five steps of Setting Up . For the detailed criteria of each step, see Levelling & Sizing · Linespacing · Letterspacing ; for layout, Zoning · Margin · Compound Grid ; for other languages and alternative typefaces, Multilingual . Line Unit — the base leading of the page. The unit that sets every distance in the layout. Level — a tier of text divided by role. Each has four parameters: multiple (x) · weight · linespacing · letterspacing Linespacing — the ratio of leading to type size. 140% means the leading is 1.4 times the type size Tonal value — the brightness of a block of text seen from a distance. The criterion for balance between levels

The Line Unit is the base unit of the page. Set the leading of every level as a multiple of the Line Unit; the actual type size is the leading divided by the linespacing (%). From here on, the Line Unit is abbreviated as x: values written in x are multiples of the Line Unit, and values written in % are all linespacing ratios. For example, 2.5x means the leading of that level is set at 2.5 times the Line Unit. As a rule, base the Line Unit on the content, or the component of it, that is used most widely · most often and carries the most weight on the page . In content layouts, the leading of the body level usually becomes the Line Unit. In visual communication without significant body copy (posters · banners · key visuals), set the Line Unit at 1x or 0.5x the height of the symbol. The recommended Line Unit for web and editorial environments is 28px. Adjust it at the designer's discretion to suit the page size and the reader's viewing distance. Once the Line Unit is set, subtract the top and bottom margins from the full height of the content area, set a baseline grid in whole multiples of the Line Unit, and reuse it across content in the same series. For details on grid and margin, see Margin and Compound Grid .

A seven-level preset based on Line Unit 1x = 28px. The first letter of a level name is the role of its content: D for display, H for headline, T for text, C for caption. This web guideline is set in four of these levels, H1 · H3 · T1 · C1; refer to the unused ones when creating new levels. Each level specifies multiple (x) · weight · linespacing · letterspacing, and the size in parentheses is the type size rendered on screen at 1x = 28px. D1 — 6x / Medium / 80% / -2.5%. One or two words, such as a tagline or core keyword, on a poster or key visual H1 — 2.5x / Medium / 100% / -1.5% (70px). Main headline · page title D2 — 2.5x / Regular / 100% / -2% (70px). Display at headline level, campaign slogan · sub copy · quotation H2 — 2x / Regular / 115% / -1% (49px). Sub-headline H3 — 1.25x / Regular / 125% / -0.5% Solid Gray · 0 Space Black (28px). Section head · subhead T1 — 1x / Light / 140% / +1% Solid Gray · +1.5% Space Black (20px). Body > brand communication first T2 — 1x / Light / 150% / +1.5% Solid Gray · +2% Space Black (18.67px). Body > readability first C1 — 0.5x / Mono Regular / 111% / -7% (12.6px). Caption · label · tag · spec · date · button The recommended weight for each level follows these criteria: Medium for display and headlines (D1 · H1), Regular for sub-display and sub-headlines (D2 · H2 · H3), Light for body copy (T1), Mono Regular for informational text (C1). Use Founders Grotesk Semibold only in a limited way, at the designer's discretion, for optical correction when Medium-level display text is inverted onto a light background and set small. To emphasize keywords within body copy, do not change the weight; use the Builder Neon color with an underline. Set level multiples in steps of 1x · 0.5x · 0.25x, and refine linespacing and letterspacing so that the tonal value carries consistently from each level to its neighbors. For the adjusted values for Korean and Vietnamese, see Multilingual . Founders Grotesk has narrow apertures and tight letterspacing, so at body level set it in Light with generous linespacing and slightly opened letterspacing. The presets are designed with a focus on visual communication: we recommend T1 for content where the text read in one go runs to only a few paragraphs, and T2 where the readability of body copy matters most. All the presets above assume Air White text on a Solid Gray background. For Space Black text on Air White · Builder Neon backgrounds, see Inversion .

How to set up typography in a new medium or format. This is less a fixed sequence than a process of converging on the best result by tuning steps 3-4 against each other. Decide the number of typography levels. Decide which levels to use based on the amount of information shown on the page. For details, see Levelling & Sizing . Set the Line Unit and set a baseline grid in the content area of the page. As a rule, size the Line Unit from the content, or the component of it, that carries the most weight or occupies the most space on the page. For details on the Line Unit, see Line Unit ; for grid setting, Margin · Compound Grid . Place the content on the grid and set the hierarchy with each level's multiple. Set the multiples in steps of 1x · 0.5x · 0.25x. For details, see Levelling & Sizing . Starting from the values in Reference Scale and adjusting them to the medium also works well. Refine weight · linespacing · letterspacing · color · line breaks for each level to match the tonal value. Tonal value is the brightness of a block of text seen from a distance; it is right when every level looks like the same text enlarged · reduced, at the same brightness. Place the levels side by side and squint, or zoom the screen out, and the differences show. As a rule, the larger the type, the lower the linespacing; the smaller the type, the higher. For details, see Linespacing . Repeat steps 3-4 until the levels reach a balance in which they look consistently enlarged · reduced according to the hierarchy. 1 Decide the number of levels 2 Set the Line Unit and set a baseline grid in the content area. 3 Place the content on the grid and set the hierarchy with each level's multiple 4 Match linespacing and tonal value 5 Repeat steps 3-4 to complete the layout

Divide levels by the role of the content. The one or two words that represent the page are display (D), the point where reading starts is headline (H), the text read down the page is text (T), and the information supporting the text is caption (C). Numbers within a role run in order of size. Number of levels — Headline and body, or headline · body · caption. Dividing levels by role is the default, but the difficulty of keeping typography consistent rises steeply with too many levels, so first consider whether information of similar role and priority can be merged into one level. Contrast between levels — The look and feel of typography is largely decided by the degree of contrast between adjacent levels. For roles to be told apart at a glance, the step from body (1x) to headline must be at least double (2-3x), and so must the step from headline to display. Within a role that handles detailed content (H2 → H3), a multiple of about 1.5 is appropriate. Keep all multiples to steps of 1x · 0.5x · 0.25x so that they fit the baseline grid. Symbol and levels — Treat the symbol like a level. Setting 1x or 0.5x of the symbol height as the Line Unit ties the symbol and the typography to the same unit. The size of the symbol follows Symbol › Scalability . As a rule, the larger the level, the heavier the weight and the tighter the linespacing and letterspacing. In practice, though, levelling is less a linear procedure in table-of-contents order than a process of tuning Linespacing · Letterspacing · weight against each other at the same time. For the preset values, see Reference Scale .

Linespacing is the height of the space one line of type occupies divided by the type size, expressed in % as in common office software. In the same space, lower linespacing makes the type larger. It corresponds to Line height % in Figma, line-height in CSS and Auto Leading in InDesign. Linespacing can vary with format and type of communication; for the presets by level, see Reference Scale . Headlines and display have linespacing of 100% or less, that is, leading equal to or tighter than the type size. Avoid extremely loose or tight linespacing, and where possible also consider revising part of the copy.

The linespacing of sub-headlines (H2 · H3) sits between headline and body (115-125%). They often run to 2-4 lines, so apply wider leading than headlines to raise readability somewhat. D2, the Regular at headline size, follows the same leading rule as headlines. Sub-headlines often sit directly above body copy, so also check that their leading does not fall out of step with the body's baseline grid.

Body copy creates its reading rhythm with leading wider than the type size. The longer a line, the more leading it needs, so the eye does not lose the next line. Too wide, though, and the lines drift apart, the paragraph scatters and the visual finish suffers. Within the range that secures readability without strain, tighten the leading little by little until a consistent gray mass forms. In content-centered layouts, the leading of the body copy becomes the Line Unit . Changing the body's Line Unit stretches or shrinks the whole digital layout vertically at the same ratio.

Captions · labels · tags · specs (C1) are short, one or two lines, with small type. Mono has wide letters and a large x-height, so with leading as open as body copy the lines look as if they float; set it at a tighter ratio than body copy. The leading of C1 is half the Line Unit. Two lines of caption equal the height of one line of body copy, so informational text also sits on the same baseline grid.

In large type the spaces between letters look larger too, so tighten the letterspacing. The reference point is where the letters sit together like one block but the strokes stop just short of touching (some horizontally open glyphs may touch each other). Too tight, and combinations of consecutive vertical strokes read as one mass; too loose, and words scatter into letters and the headline loses its weight.

Because the inherent tonal value of Regular is lower than that of Medium, securing a tonal value at sub-headline level close to that of the headline level calls for relatively tighter letterspacing. For example, H1 uses Medium at -1.5% letterspacing, while D2, at the same type size, applies an even tighter -2%.

In small type the spaces look relatively small, so open the letterspacing to around 1-1.5%, taking light text on a dark background as the reference. Because the thin weight loses readability quickly when the letterspacing is tightened, find the compromise according to which matters more, uniform tonal value or readability.

By nature, Mono is highly distinguishable even at small sizes, but its readability as running text is low, so tighten the letterspacing to around -7%. If many long words make the lines run long, consider switching to the body typeface.

Content in EO brand communication is left aligned by default. Center alignment is allowed only when the text is a single line, as with standalone symbol icons and merch back prints; do not use justified text. When body copy runs in several columns, align the first-line baselines of all columns. Align the symbol left to the image's left edge and the caption right to its right edge. A single left alignment line becomes the reference line of the page: headline · sub-headline · body start from the same line, and the reader starts reading at the same place on every line. Right alignment loses that reference because the start of each line moves, and justified text opens the word spaces and makes the tonal value uneven. This rule applies to every weight. The exception is informational text (C1 · Mono). A caption beneath an image may be right aligned to the right edge, paired with the symbol left aligned to the left edge, and a caption attached to a simple graphic such as an icon · shape · illustration may be center aligned above or below it. All other Mono text is left aligned like the other levels, and justified text is not used for Mono either. Headline (Medium) — left aligned by default; center · right · justified are not used Sub-headline (Regular) — same rule as the headline Body (Light) — same rule as the headline Informational text (Mono) — captions at an image edge may be right aligned and captions of simple icons · shapes may be center aligned. Justified is never used

A paragraph has a bad rag when its edge feels irregular, when a particular line sticks out, or when a single word is left alone on the last line. Headlines are short with few lines, so the rag shows plainly. Break lines so that each line holds a unit of meaning, as in "Build / Anyway.", and avoid the staircase shape of alternating long and short lines. In body copy, move words to the next line until the edge is even and the copy reads well.

Divide the page into a graphic pattern area and a content area. Ideally the graphic pattern area is close to a square on 3:4 · A-series · business card formats, takes around 70% of the page on horizontal wide formats, and around half on vertical roll-ups. Communication pages with little information may also be divided into four, with content alternating with the pattern or gathered to one side. Typography in the content area runs left and top aligned, so when splitting the page side by side, prefer placing the graphic pattern area on the right; when splitting it top and bottom, at the top. Place the graphic pattern area full bleed, ignoring the margin, and arrange its units following Graphic Pattern › Zoning . For the boundary between the two areas, set the Compound Grid first, check the right proportion of the areas against its columns · rows, and align the boundary to the nearest line. If it does not fall exactly on a line, adjust it to the midline of a column · row or to a baseline. The content area is what remains, and the margin is set from this area. In a four-way division, use one of the divided content areas as the reference. For pages whose front and back are linked, such as business cards, use the side that carries the main content. Examples of the proportion between graphic pattern area and content area Four-way division, with content and graphic pattern areas alternating diagonally or gathered to one side

Set the margin of the content area equal on all four sides, based on 1/24 of the area's long side; we recommend setting the horizontal margins about 10% narrower. The final value settles between 1/22 and 1/25 as the number of baseline cells is matched in Compound Grid . On pages read up close the margin is about the same scale as the Line Unit; on pages seen from a distance it can shrink to around 70-80% of the Line Unit. On a side where typography meets the graphic pattern , leave about 1.5 times the margin. The top edge of typography is a gray edge, because the tops of the letters are uneven, so compensate with more space than at crisp edges such as the left alignment line · the baseline · the left and bottom of the symbol. Text is left aligned, so its right side does not meet the pattern. Margin — 1/24 of the content area's long side, equal on all four sides, or with the horizontal margins corrected about 10% narrower Margin next to the pattern corrected to 1.5 times; the top of typography is a gray edge, so give it more room than the crisp left alignment line · baseline

The base grid is a baseline grid in whole multiples of the Line Unit. The margin is set first in Margin from the content area, and settles between 1/22 and 1/25 as the number of baseline cells N is matched. Then verify that the margin falls within 0.8-1.1 times the Line Unit on pages read up close, and 0.7-0.8 times on pages seen from a distance. For large pages or layouts with complex components, we recommend the Compound Grid, which combines a modular grid with this baseline grid. It is a modular grid that divides the content area evenly with gutters of one Line Unit, and since the height of a module cell is also a whole multiple of the Line Unit, it is fully compatible with the baseline grid. Compound Grid rows — The Compound Grid can be applied when the total number of baseline cells satisfies N = number of rows R × (Line Units per row n + 1) − 1 . For example, 35 cells divide into 6 rows × 5 cells or 4 rows × 8 cells. 47 cells allow 4 · 6 · 8 · 12 rows alike, making it the most flexible. With the gutter between rows widened to 2 cells, 47 cells also divide into 7 rows × 5 cells. Compound Grid columns — 12 columns × 6 rows are commonly used on 16:9 pages and 6 columns × 6 rows on A-series formats, but set the number freely at the designer's discretion. On A-series or similarly proportioned pages, set it from the page proportion so that the graphic pattern area comes close to a square. The gutter between columns is 1x the Line Unit. 47 cells — 6 rows × 7 cells · 8 rows × 5 cells · 7 rows × 5 cells (2-cell gutter), row gutters of 1-2 cells Column grid — on the same 35 cells, 12 columns for 16:9 · 6 columns for A-series, column gutter of 1x the Line Unit

EO typography is built primarily for light text, such as Air White · Medium Gray , on dark backgrounds such as Solid Gray · Space Black . As with the signature's descriptor , when you want dark text on a light background and simply invert the colors, an optical illusion occurs: at the same weight and letterspacing, the letters look thinner and the letterspacing looks wider. In that case, keep the Line Unit · level multiples · weights as they are, correct the type size to 1.05 times (linespacing 0.95 times) and apply 1% tighter letterspacing. The tonal value then stays at a consistent level on light backgrounds too, and because the space the type occupies is unchanged, layout changes are kept to a minimum. Below is an example of the same presets applied to the seven-level Reference Scale and set in light mode.

Use Pretendard for Korean and Noto Sans for Vietnamese. When an existing layout is changed to a multilingual typeface, the Line Unit and level multiples stay the same, so the layout does not move when the language changes. Below are multilingual conversions for T1 · H3 of the Reference Scale . Korean Pretendard — T1 is Regular · 165% · -1.5% · baseline +0.2x, and H3 is Medium · 165% · -2.5% · baseline -0.05x. The rendered type size is about 0.85 times that of Founders Grotesk at the same level. Vietnamese Noto Sans — T1 is DemiLight · 175% · -1% · baseline +0.05x, and H3 is Regular · 175% · -3% · baseline +0.05x. The rendered type size is about 0.8 times that of Founders Grotesk at the same level. The baseline correction is for matching positions relative to the text box in editorial design tools. In digital environments the browser aligns baselines by itself, so on the web the correction is rarely needed, but where type is shown large, as with display fonts, correct it with a separate margin inside the text box. These two typefaces are also the alternatives in environments where Founders Grotesk cannot be used (email, system-font restrictions on external platforms and document tools, and so on). In that case, set English in Pretendard first as well, and use Noto Sans where Pretendard cannot be used or does not support the language.

Below are the things not to do with typography in brand communication. To keep consistency across every touchpoint, follow the typesetting rules and recommendations of this chapter. How far individual service · product · content design prioritizes brand communication consistency is at the designer's discretion or follows the EO design team's policy. Do not stretch or distort type Do not set headlines in all caps Do not use Light for headlines or Regular · Medium for body copy Do not use two or more colors in a headline Do not center or right align headlines Do not use two or more weights within one level Do not apply outlines · italics to type Do not overlay typography on the graphic pattern Do not use Mono for headlines or body copy Do not use typefaces other than those specified Do not place text off the baseline grid

Builder Neon stands for the window of a hacker house whose lights stay on all night, and for the optimism of the builders making something inside. At night it is a signal that stays lit through a builder's loneliest hours; by day, set against the blue sky of San Francisco, it is the first mark to catch the eye.

Day Blue and Bay Green are cool tones drawn from the nature of the Bay Area. Day Blue takes its cue from the crisp air of San Francisco, Bay Green from the greenery of the chaparral hills that run along the coastal ridges. As supporting colors, both make their complement, Builder Neon , appear even more vivid.

The EO palette consists of Builder Neon · Day Blue · Bay Green and four neutral colors that support them. Solid Gray and Medium Gray carry the neutral stance of a media brand: use the darker one as a background color and the lighter one for graphic elements. Space Black and Air White are the foundation for backgrounds and text. Each color is specified in HEX · RGB for screen and in CMYK · Pantone for print. Use the color mode that matches the medium. In print, Air White can be left as unprinted white paper. Builder Neon #F9EE3A Day Blue #6EC6D2 Bay Green #66B88A Medium Gray #8E8E8E Solid Gray #2A2B2B Space Black #000000 Air White #FCFBF5

Use Solid Gray or Space Black as the default background; in media that allow photography, the San Francisco sky itself becomes the background. For graphic elements placed on the background, the recommended ratio is Builder Neon 50%, Day Blue · Bay Green 30%, and Medium Gray · Air White 20%. Set text mainly in Air White · Space Black, at around 10% of the overall composition. In text-led media, the share of background rises; in pattern-led media, the share of Builder Neon rises. In contexts where the EO brand is already clearly recognized, such as social channels or series artwork, Day Blue · Bay Green may be used more freely than the recommended ratio allows. For detailed application by element, see the Color section of each page. Logo For color use of the symbol, see Symbol › Color . For color use of the signature, see Signature › Color . For color use of the sub symbol, see Sub Symbol › Color . Graphic system For color use of the graphic unit, see Graphic Unit › Color . For color use of the pattern, see Graphic Pattern › Color .
The following images show the EO palette applied across a range of designs. 1 Outdoor flag 2 Hanging banner 3 Poster 4 Clothing

To keep EO's colors consistent, avoid the following. For the minimum contrast between text and background, refer to the WCAG guidelines. Do not use Builder Neon for all body text or for text on light backgrounds Do not create gradients Do not add colors outside the palette (request them from the EO design team if needed) Do not use unapproved color combinations Do not use low-contrast combinations such as Day Blue · Bay Green · Medium Gray Do not create new tones by changing brightness · saturation · opacity (request them from the EO design team if needed)

Like the EO symbol , the EO graphic unit (hereafter, the unit) takes its motif from the three parts of a screw: shaft · thread · head. Thread — One turn of the thread symbolizes one cycle of problem solving. The harder the wall it meets, the stronger the resistance and the longer it takes to break through. The tighter the threads, the more densely the builder's time is filled (Build through). Shaft — The shaft symbolizes the process of building and the builder's journey. The shaft size expresses how strong the core qualities of that process are. The thicker the shaft, the stronger the push forward (Build anyway). Head — The head symbolizes one small problem solved, or one builder. Many small screws together can build anything (Build anything). Likewise, a problem one builder cannot solve is eventually solved when many builders face it together (Build together).

The EO graphic unit (hereafter, the unit) is the smallest element of the graphic system. The logo's E block, the pattern library and application graphics are all built with the same system. Units are generated from parameters in EO Graphic Builder; for detailed instructions, see the Help menu inside the tool. shaft size — The thickness of the shaft rectangle, as a percentage of the unit's total height including the threads on both sides. At around the default of 35%, the shaft size makes it easy to keep visual density ideal even in relatively complex graphic patterns. thread top, bottom width — The width of the thread's top and bottom edges. The thread is a trapezoid abstracted from a screw thread: one side stands vertically at the end of the column, the opposite side slants, and the lower thread is the upper one rotated 180° about the column center. The difference between the two values sets the thread's slope. Defaults are top 40% · bottom 0% (the top edge as a percentage of the column width, the bottom edge as the percentage taken off the column width). thread sides — With double, threads attach to both the top and bottom of the shaft; with single, threads attach to one side only and the shaft rests at the bottom. thread amount — The number of threads attached to each of the top and bottom of the shaft. thread compression — How much the thread width narrows progressively toward one side. At 0, all threads have equal width; the higher the value, the stronger the compression toward one side. Negative and positive values set the direction of compression; the slope of each thread stays as it is and does not flip. The whole unit can also be flipped horizontally, so both the tight end and the thread direction can face either way. thread gutter — The space between the vertical cells in which the threads sit. A single value applies in common to every gap between cells within a unit. In EO Graphic Builder it is labeled gutter. shaft size — shaft thickness 2-95% thread top, bottom width — change in slope thread sides — double · single thread amount — number of threads thread compression — direction · strength of thread compression thread gutter — spacing common to all threads

Color shows who the protagonist of a graphic is, what forms the environment, and where a state changes. Use it as a supporting device that complements the nuance of Vocabulary. For more specific combination rules, see Graphic Pattern › Color . Apply only one color to each unit. Builder Neon — The main color, highest in hierarchy, expressing the nuance of the builder · protagonist · focus · highlighting. It works best when it covers 20-50% of the whole page. Air White — A neutral color, high in hierarchy but without identity, expressing the nuance of energy · the counterpart · semi-highlighting. It works best when it covers 10-30% of the whole page. Day Blue — Builders of a different character · community · surrounding elements. Emphasizes the nuance of positive energy · optimism drawn from a blue sky. Bay Green — Builders of a different character · community · surrounding elements. Emphasizes the nuance of softness · friendliness drawn from the green of California's chaparral hills. Medium Gray — Expresses the nuance of mechanical neutrality: inactivity · the other · indifference · conservatism · the material world. Space Black — As a unit color, use it sparingly rather than freely, so that it secures visual hierarchy when needed. For situations where visual impact comes first, a combination with a Builder Neon background is recommended, expressing overwhelming presence. Solid Gray is not used as a unit color. Builder Neon builder · protagonist · focus, Air White energy · counterpart · semi-highlighting Day Blue other builders · surrounding elements · optimism, Bay Green other builders · surrounding elements · friendliness Medium Gray inactivity · the other · conservatism · the material world Space Black on Builder Neon recommended combination, overwhelming presence

A unit takes on new meaning through its direction, number and density alone. The shaft, for example, is the passage of time and the thread a unit of problem solving, so the more tightly threads gather in a narrow stretch, the harder and longer the time they express. The visual intensity of that stretch naturally grows with it. When a parameter-based shape and the value the brand wants to convey point in the same direction like this, we call it visual-to-brand mapping . Vocabulary is the dictionary of the EO graphic system that collects these mapping rules. It gives comprehensive guidance on which visual properties and colors to combine to express a given value keyword. The rules below are those defined so far, not a complete set; new metaphors can be added at any time. This section mainly covers keyword expression; for guidance on visual quality, see Morphology and Graphic Pattern › Grammar . For docking, the way two units are aligned, see Docking .

A thread is one turn of a screw thread and stands for one act of problem solving. How tight the threads are within a unit · which way they lean · how long they run express the character of that time. Keywords expressed with thread: adversity · acceleration · spark · builder. Adversity — A time of difficulty, resistance from the environment. Expressed by laying the unit horizontally. Tighter threads express greater difficulty; which end is tighter shows whether the hardest stretch comes at the start or at the end. Acceleration — A change in thread density can feel like acceleration, a stretch where momentum builds. When compression loosens in the direction of travel, it reads as acceleration; when it tightens instead, it can read as deceleration. Units repeated end to end can also read as a recurring, routine-like flow. Spark — Lightning · inspiration · energy. When the shaft is long enough and the thread compression spreads relatively gently, the unit can resemble a bolt of lightning. Use only Builder Neon · Air White for this metaphor. Builder — A single builder · person · entity. Expressed by standing the unit vertically. Compression tightens the bottom, and the direction in which the upper threads lean is the direction the figure faces. Use Builder Neon for a unit that represents EO or the protagonist, Air White for a unit with a stake in the story but not the protagonist, Day Blue · Bay Green for peers · friends, and Medium Gray for others · hostile presences. Adversity — threads tightening along the timeline Acceleration — threads that widen in the direction of travel Spark — long, thin threads with gentle compression Builder — compression weighted at the bottom, as if standing on the ground

The shaft is the axis of the screw and symbolizes the timeline of the building process; the shaft size expresses how strong the core qualities of that process are. Keywords expressed with shaft: growth · diversity · backing. Growth — Conviction · magnitude of strength. Expressed by three or more shafts thickening step by step. Diversity — Differences in character. Expressed by placing several units with different shaft sizes side by side in random order. The larger the shaft size, the shorter the threads, so each unit's impression changes markedly; the nuance is not that thicker is always better, but that each has its own character. Use an even mix of unit colors . Backing — The side that bears or receives weight. With threads on one side only, the shaft on that side becomes the ground and the threads stand on it; the taller the threads and the steeper their slope, the more dramatic the expression. Make the shaft of the supporting unit below thick and the unit above thin, so the relationship of bearing weight is clear. Apply Builder Neon to the unit that represents EO or the protagonist. Growth — shafts thickening step by step Diversity — several units of varying shaft size placed side by side in random order Backing — a unit with a thick shaft supporting a thin unit from below

Connecting two units creates a new relationship. Different contexts arise from whether they combine horizontally or vertically, and whether they face the same or opposite directions. Keywords expressed with pair: journey · momentum · pulse · peers · rivals · house. Journey — Length of time, a recurring process. Expressed by docking two horizontal units with the same compression direction. It shows one chapter ending and the next beginning; repeated, it becomes a routine · cycle. Apply the same color to a docked unit pair. Momentum — The moment acceleration crosses a threshold and changes direction. Expressed by inverting two horizontal units about the center and docking them at the ends where their threads are loosest. Adjust compression so that in both states the eye is drawn to the middle. Pulse — Wave · frequency · a spreading signal. Expressed by inverting two spark units with point or mirror symmetry and joining them at the ends where their threads are loosest. Peers — Two figures standing together. Expressed by standing two vertical units side by side, facing the same direction. Apply Builder Neon to the unit representing EO or the protagonist, and another color that suits the peer's character to the peer unit. Rivals — Opposition · competition. Expressed by standing two vertical units side by side, facing each other. Apply Builder Neon to the unit representing EO or the protagonist, and Air White · Medium Gray to the rival unit. House — Shelter · community · EO House. Expressed by standing two vertical units side by side, facing outward, so their silhouette forms a roof. For EO House, apply Builder Neon to both units, or Builder Neon to the left unit and Day Blue to the right. Journey · routine — docked in the same direction Momentum — two states docked after center inversion Pulse — two spark units docked with point · mirror symmetry Peers — two vertical units, same direction Rivals — two vertical units, facing each other House — roof silhouette (EO House)

Extending the metaphors so far into larger arrangements expresses the relationships · spaces · worlds · dimensions they belong to. Keywords expressed with Formation: scale · dimension · direction · radiation · crossing. Scale — Multiple entities · processes · states. Repeat an existing metaphor. Consider using color even more actively: a single Builder Neon among many Medium Gray units, for example, is the protagonist within them. Dimension — Parallel worlds. Blend a pair in geometric progression. If one line is a single timeline, stacked lines become multidimensional space-time or parallel worlds. A single Builder Neon among Medium Gray timelines is the present timeline. Direction — Expresses drive · flow. Place units, inverted so that the negative space between them takes the shape of arrows, in parallel along the shaft axis, so that the arrows point regularly to one side. Radiation — Bursting energy · resonance. Mirror the directional pattern above. Consider Builder Neon at the source of the energy. Crossing — Simultaneous · instantaneous sync. Stack spark units in alternating order, placing their vertices · edges with tension. Scale — extending the metaphor of the same unit · group Dimension — space-time · parallel worlds Direction — drive · flow Radiation — bursting energy · resonance Crossing — simultaneous · instantaneous sync

Any unit can be made easily with a few parameters, but a well-formed unit comes from proportion and rhythm, not from absolute values. Vocabulary covers the meanings and metaphors that units and pairs carry. Morphology covers how a word with the same meaning should ideally look: the proportion and rhythm of a single unit. This section provides a checklist for visually ideal units and recommended parameter ranges. These are not absolute standards; let the designer's aesthetic judgment decide the final parameter values. For rules on combining multiple units, see Graphic Pattern › Grammar .

A defining feature of the EO graphic unit is that its size and aspect ratio can be transformed freely. Not every proportion, however, works visually. We recommend units that read as long along the shaft axis. When the shaft turns squat, all the threads bunch together, which does not suit the intended metaphor. As an exception, units used within a complex pattern · at its periphery may take a squat shape. Units that are thin and long like a straight line along the shaft axis are not ideal either. The threads stretch along the long shaft until the original metaphor is no longer recognizable, and formally the gutters grow excessive, so avoid them. Unit that reads as moderately long along the shaft axis Squat unit widened perpendicular to the axis, its threads bunched together Unit whose moderately long shaft is balanced like a body Unit whose shaft stretches into a thin line, its threads stretched long with it

Raising the compression value tightens the threads toward one side and creates rhythm. In general, we recommend an absolute compression value of 1.5-2.5. When thread proportion and spacing are constant, the rhythm turns monotonous; the unit looks flat, like stripes, and struggles to create visual interest. Only with enough compression do the threads form a rhythm and gain movement. As tight lines converge on the unit's edge, they create visual tension and deliberately bring flow to a still plane. With too much compression, threads squeezed to hairline thickness repeat at the tight end and become just as dull. In that case, reduce the thread amount or lower the compression slightly to cut the repetitions. Or lower the thread gutter so the stretch merges into a single gray band, which largely offsets the repetitive feel. Short units tend to avoid monotony even with a small thread amount and mild compression, because each thread's shape stands out. Long units, by contrast, reach a good rhythm with a large thread amount and strong compression. Compression that creates a good rhythm Monotonous unit with constant spacing Thread amount and compression suited to a long unit Unit made monotonous by mild compression Compression that converges on the edge and creates movement Unit with excessive compression, hairlines repeating at one end

Seen up close · large, each thread reads as a distinct shape; seen from afar · small, adjacent shapes merge into a gray mass of even density. The edge of the gray mass changes with compression, and its density with the thread gutter and thread slope. The thread gutter is the spacing applied in common between all threads within a unit, and it decides whether tight threads read as individual lines or merge into a gray mass. For digital assets at typical resolutions, we recommend a thread gutter of about 10-20px. Tight stretches almost always look better merged into a gray mass. Rather than exposing threads that repeat evenly at hairline thickness, lower the thread gutter so the stretch merges into a narrow band at the end of the unit. For digital assets at typical resolutions, the thread gutter rarely goes above 30px. A Space Black unit shrinks visually on a light background, and the gray mass at the tight end can scatter into individual threads, breaking the original rhythm. When inverting from a light to a dark color (or the reverse), reset the thread gutter and compression. Tight stretch merged into a gray mass by a small thread gutter Stretch where a large thread gutter makes each hairline stand out Unit with thread gutter and compression reset on inversion Unit with values left unchanged and only the color inverted

The difference between the widths of the thread's top and bottom edges. It determines the thread's sharpness and the area it occupies, and affects the tonal value of tight compression stretches. A thread whose diagonal takes up about 60% of its area is ideal, so we recommend a thread top width of 35-50% and a bottom width of 0-20%. A thicker shaft makes the threads shorter and their slope gentler. When adjusting the shaft size, keep in mind that the thread slope moves with it. The more units a pattern holds, the more the threads merge into a gray mass rather than reading as individual slopes. Keep thread top, bottom width within the recommended range where possible, and adjust it only to fine-tune tonal value. Close-ups with thread sides set to single are the exception, since there the thread slope becomes the key metaphor. Thread at top 40% · bottom 10% Thread with top · bottom outside the recommended range

Docking is the way to handle the seam when two units of the same color are joined along the shaft axis to form one long unit. At the joint, the thread spacing must continue the rhythm of both sides, which requires the two units to share the same shaft size and thread gutter. Simply butting them together removes the spacing at the seam and makes the thread rhythm jump. Docking that carries the rhythm through the seam Two units butted together without docking, the rhythm broken at the seam

A unit's meaning and aesthetics come from the changing density of threads spread across a plane, so when that plane is disturbed, the rhythm created by compression easily collapses with it. Make every change to the unit's geometry within the parameters of EO Graphic Builder, and avoid manual transformation wherever possible. However, three-dimensional extensions that project the entire plane holding the unit isometrically or in perspective may be attempted on a limited basis, after review by the EO design team. Do not rotate the unit at angles other than multiples of 90° Do not arbitrarily distort the unit's shape Do not apply more than one color to a unit Do not use Solid Gray as a unit color; it is reserved for backgrounds Do not join two units along the shaft axis (docking) when their shaft sizes do not match Projecting the unit onto a three-dimensional plane

The EO graphic system is built in three layers, like a language. Vocabulary is the words. It covers what units and pairs mean: their significance and metaphors. Morphology is the form of the word. Even when the meaning stays the same, it covers how a unit should ideally look: the proportion and rhythm of a single unit. Grammar is the set of rules that turns words into sentences. It is the layout rules for placing multiple units on one page. Vocabulary covers what a unit means and Morphology covers how it looks, so the Grammar section deals with layout form rather than meaning. The library in References shows representative examples of these rules in action; designers can reinterpret them to create new patterns.

To build a new layout, first build the Compound Grid, then use the modular grid as the primary guide to divide the page into the graphic pattern area and the content area, and finally complete the pattern inside the graphic pattern area. For detailed guidance on the Compound Grid, see Compound Grid . Do not set a margin between the two areas explicitly; treat it as part of the content area's margin. The graphic pattern area is a rectangular area that corresponds to the Frame in EO Graphic Builder. Stacking units inside it, interlocked like Tetris pieces with no empty space, is a separate system. Unit placement inside the graphic pattern area does not need to align with the typography grid. The two systems, the graphic pattern area and the typography-led content area, create a contrast between strong and soft on a single page. Because typography in the content area runs left and top aligned, prefer placing the graphic pattern area on the right when splitting the page side by side, and at the top when splitting it top and bottom. The exception is vertical media that stand on the ground or hang from a pole, such as roll-up banners · hanging banners, where placing the pattern at the bottom can suit better. Set the side with dense compression against the ground so the unit reads as a builder or house standing on the ground; the dense threads then evoke the ground (see Builder ). When drafting graphics for a new metaphor in the EO Graphic Builder workspace, you set up an independent grid inside the Frame and place graphic units on it in a regular order. This is a separate system, entirely independent of the Compound Grid that this guideline focuses on. Areas divided in ideal proportion A graphic pattern area that is too small, with a graphic pattern competing for hierarchy with other elements A graphic pattern area divided along columns and rows A layout with the graphic pattern area placed at the left or bottom

Set the pattern margin to 0 so the pattern fills 100% of the graphic pattern area on the page. The graphic pattern area extends past the page margin and fills up to the edge of the page. Placing a stretch of tight compression in a unit against the edge of the page creates the illusion that the unit enters from, or reaches beyond, the page, adding visual interest. As an exception, a piece made of the graphic pattern alone, with no content area, can take a margin similar to the pattern gutter. A graphic pattern that strengthens its metaphor by placing the compressed end of a graphic unit at the edge of the page A graphic pattern in a content layout that does not fill 100% to the margin

The pattern gutter is the space between units within a graphic pattern. Set it based on unit density and the size of the thinnest thread; tighter is generally better. Balance the pattern gutter with the thread gutter . A well-set pattern gutter keeps the eye fully on the visual elements of the graphic pattern and builds visual tension. Set the pattern gutter to about 1.5 times the thread gutter. For typical digital assets, the thread gutter stays between 10 and 20px, so a pattern gutter of 20-25px is ideal. When needed, set the pattern gutter to 0 so units touch. Using the pattern gutter irregularly to overlap units has potential for experimental patterns, but it introduces too many variables; avoid it for now. A pattern gutter balanced with the thread gutter A pattern gutter out of balance with the thread gutter Inconsistent pattern gutters within one pattern Overlapping units has potential, but avoid it for now

There are no specific restrictions on combining horizontal and vertical units, but keeping each unit's form close to the recommendations in Morphology helps create a fluid pattern. Once the units are aligned in the graphic pattern area, look closely at the shaft and thread lines that happen to form between intersecting units. Unintended misalignment can undermine the quality of the entire pattern. Fine-tune the compression of vertical units and the shaft size of horizontal units so the shaft lines of horizontal units line up with the thread lines of vertical units. We recommend this as the final step in completing a layout. A pattern where the thread lines of crossing units are misaligned A pattern where the thread lines of crossing units are deliberately aligned A pattern with shaft and thread lines deliberately aligned A pattern with misaligned lines, or offsets whose intent is unclear

By default, use Builder Neon · Air White · Day Blue · Bay Green · Medium Gray as unit colors , and Solid Gray · Space Black as background colors. When placing several units side by side, either arrange Day Blue · Bay Green · Medium Gray, which are close in lightness, with even weight · position · movement, or use the brighter Builder Neon · Air White as focal points to deliberately control the sense of depth on the page. Use Builder Neon as a background color, with Space Black units on top, only on pages that must project the brand's presence most strongly and carry little information. Unit color Apply only one color to each unit. We recommend no more than three unit colors at once in one graphic pattern; up to four are allowed only for the fixed combination of Builder Neon · Day Blue · Bay Green · Medium Gray. Medium Gray is a supporting color; combining it with units in other colors is the default. Only when deliberately depicting a negative situation, such as resistance · stagnation, may a pattern be composed of Medium Gray alone. Do not use Solid Gray as a unit color. Background color Consider Solid Gray first as a background color: it lowers the contrast with all five unit colors by one step, holding every color together calmly. Consider a Space Black background next. On Builder Neon · Day Blue · Bay Green · Air White backgrounds, use only Space Black units. Do not use Medium Gray as a background color in digital environments. For merch, only when the physical material's color can be matched to Medium Gray, Builder Neon · Space Black units may be used on it in limited cases, with approval from the EO design team. The Do · Don't examples below form a reference chart that gathers, on one sheet, the unit colors allowed on each background color. The number of colors actually used in one pattern follows the rules above. Builder Neon · Day Blue · Bay Green · Medium Gray · Air White on Solid Gray Builder Neon · Day Blue · Bay Green · Medium Gray · Air White on Space Black Space Black on Builder Neon · Day Blue · Bay Green · Air White Builder Neon · Space Black on Medium Gray Medium Gray alone on Solid Gray · Space Black Space Black on Solid Gray or vice versa Day Blue · Bay Green · Medium Gray · Air White on Builder Neon Builder Neon · Bay Green · Medium Gray · Air White on Day Blue Builder Neon · Day Blue · Medium Gray · Air White on Bay Green Builder Neon · Day Blue · Bay Green · Medium Gray on Air White Day Blue · Bay Green · Air White on Medium Gray

A library of 30 patterns built by combining units. Each pattern is named not by a number but by a keyword drawn from the builder's journey, and can be used across every touchpoint: campaigns · merch · social · video and more. Designers are free to extend the keywords and create new graphics, but adding a pattern to the official library requires approval from the EO design team. 01 Path of Builder 02 Power 03 Resistance 04 Builders 05 Rivals 06 Team 07 Backing 08 Teamwork 09 Co-working 10 Rallying 11 Conviction 12 Resonance 13 Advantage 14 Disadvantage 15 Cycle 16 Routine 17 Competition 18 Collective Intelligence 19 Growth 20 Diversity 21 Momentum 22 Problem 23 A-ha 24 Wow 25 Real World 26 Singularity 27 Multi-dimension 28 Adventure 29 Nature 30 Boom

The graphic pattern is the most vivid and dense visual element in all of EO's visual expression, so it plays the protagonist, drawing the eye on the page. Give one side of the page (usually the right or top, about 70%) entirely to it as a rectangular area, set the headline left aligned at the edge of the content area on the opposite side, and place the logo in a corner of the content area. You can crop a pattern, but crop at a column boundary so the diagonal sections of a thread are not cut midway. The following are typical cases where the pattern loses its role as protagonist. Stretching or distorting a pattern breaks the proportion of its units, and placing something on a pattern, or a pattern on something, makes the two elements compete for hierarchy. Masking or repeating a pattern breaks down the rhythm created by unit density, and a pattern too complex for its display size turns its threads into an illegible blur. Do not stretch or distort the pattern Do not overlay content such as the symbol or text on the pattern Do not place the pattern over photos or other graphics Do not mask the graphic pattern area into a circle or freeform shape Do not tile the pattern as a background texture Do not use a pattern that is too complex for its display size on the page

This page is a set of reference drafts that apply the EO graphic system to various media. Refer to the look and feel, layout composition and media-specific direction of the applied graphic pattern, but actual production may differ by medium and specification, so give priority to the rules in each chapter and proceed with the approval of the EO design team. When placing the graphic pattern on a page, we recommend following these rules. Match the pattern's density to viewing distance. On large pages seen from afar, such as billboards, push complexity all the way up to hold the eye through density ; keep posters seen up close at medium complexity, and business cards held in the hand simpler still. Lead the eye with the direction of the threads . Arrange the threads so that their compression gathers in one place, leading the eye to the mark or message there. Rebuild the pattern to fit the format. Every graphic pattern is a responsive system that can be rearranged to the proportion of its rectangular area, but when stretching or shrinking the same pattern, check that the threads in the compression section have not become too dense.

Digital touchpoints such as the web · Instagram feed · SNS profile · YouTube channel. The grid system in this guideline is based mainly on static pages, so web and digital content, whose screen sizes vary, should give priority to a responsive layout suited to each environment. 1 Web UI  2 Instagram Feed            3 SNS Profile 4 YouTube Channel

Printed media such as business cards · posters · billboards · hanging banners. Color combinations follow Graphic Pattern › Color : prefer Solid Gray · Space Black backgrounds, and use a Builder Neon background sparingly to assert the brand's presence strongly. Print with the CMYK values in EO Palette . Screen RGB · HEX values shift in print, so build print files in CMYK mode from the start. Where color fidelity matters, or a Builder Neon background covers a large area, print it as a Pantone spot color. Air White can be replaced by white paper instead of ink. The same values look different on different papers and materials, so check the colors with a proof before the final run. On small pages whose front and back work together, such as business cards, put the graphic pattern on one side and the information on the other, and base the margins and grid on the side with the main content ( Zoning ). Outdoor media such as billboards · hanging banners, read from afar and in a short time, give the graphic pattern area generous room as in the examples in Graphic Pattern › Zoning , and reduce the message to about one to three lines of headline. Decide the pattern density by weighing both visual impact and viewing distance, and set the symbol size by the ratio to viewing distance in Symbol › Scalability . On vertical media that stand on the ground or hang from a pole, such as hanging banners, the graphic pattern area can sit at the bottom. 1 Billboard 2 Hanging Banner 3 Poster 4 Business Card

A brand merch line of apparel such as tees · hoodies · caps, plus hang tags · stickers · pin badges. On the tee, place a small EO symbol on the front chest and a large dedicated graphic of simplified units on the back; on the hoodie, place a pattern that blends a pair at an equal ratio ( Dimension ) on the front. For apparel graphics, screen printing is recommended so that vivid single colors stand out. Mix the inks to the Pantone values in EO Palette . Screen printing struggles with very thin lines and gradients, so instead of dense patterns whose threads get too thin, use graphics of simplified units. Treat the fabric color as the graphic's background color and follow the combinations in Graphic Pattern › Color . When printing light ink on dark fabric, lay down a white underbase first for full color. Always keep the symbol on apparel small and compact, and prefer heat-transfer printing, which carries the crisp graphic as it is. This is because embroidery brings out a strongly analog mood. For merch rendered in the color of its material, such as metal · engraving, apply the form alone instead of a color combination, and always render it in a single color. For paper accessories such as hang tags · stickers, print colors follow the standards in Print . 1 Oversized Tee 2 Hoodie 3 5-panel Cap 4 Hang Tag 5 Sticker Pack 6 Pin Badge
